sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Foundational Principle 1**: First time the British Parliament assumed the right to **regulate and control** EIC's Indian territories, ending unbridled corporate governance.
• **Foundational Principle 2**: Transformed the **Governor of Bengal** into the **Governor-General of Bengal**, subordinating the Presidencies of Bombay and Madras to Bengal.
• **Foundational Principle 3**: Established the **Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta (1774)** comprising a Chief Justice and three puisne judges to dispense English law.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Financial crisis of EIC in 1772 (seeking a £1.4 million loan from the British Crown) served as the immediate economic trigger for parliamentary intervention.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Governor of Bengal upgraded to Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings). Assisted by a 4-member Executive Council.
Decisions made by majority vote; Governor-General had only a casting vote, leading to deadlock.
Often tested in Prelims regarding executive checks and balances and executive-council friction.
Bombay and Madras presidencies made subordinate to the Bengal Presidency in matters of war and peace.
Required prior sanction of Governor-General-in-Council except in cases of imminent urgency.
Marks the historical genesis of a unified territorial administration in British India.
Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta established in 1774 (Sir Elijah Impey as first Chief Justice).
Jurisdiction over all British subjects and civil/criminal/admiralty cases in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
Source of massive friction between the Supreme Court and Governor-General's Council due to undefined jurisdiction.
Prohibited EIC servants from engaging in private trade or accepting bribes, presents, and donations from Indians.
Designed to curb rampant personal enrichment of Company officials while the EIC faced bankruptcy.
Highlights early legislative attempts at civil service integrity and accountability.

items.definition: The supreme executive body in Bengal consisting of the Governor-General and four councillors. Decisions by majority vote frequently paralyzed Warren Hastings' administration.
The governing body of the EIC based in London. The Act mandated them to report all civil, revenue, and military affairs in India to the British Crown (Treasury and Secretary of State).
Established under the 1773 Act (operational in 1774). Its ambiguous relationship with the Governor-General's Council led to major jurisdictional clashes (e.g., the Patna Case, Cossijurah Case).
The mechanism by which the British Parliament demanded accountability from the EIC regarding Indian revenues and governance, establishing ultimate parliamentary sovereignty.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Bengal Presidency**: Designated as the core administrative hub; seat of the newly minted Governor-General and the Supreme Court.
• **Subordinate Presidencies (Bombay & Madras)**: Restricted in independent foreign policy making, forcing centralization towards Calcutta.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Vague demarcation of powers between the Supreme Court and the Executive Council; majority opposition to Warren Hastings in the council (Clavering, Monson, Philip Francis).
• **Policy Interventions**: Rectified subsequently by the **Act of Settlement 1781** (which exempted revenue matters from Supreme Court jurisdiction) and **Pitt's India Act 1784**.

items.title: Mnemonic for Regulating Act Key Provisions
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'B-G-S-C' (Bengal Gets Supreme Control)
• **Decoded Meaning**: B = Bengal Governor becomes Governor-General; G = Governor-General gets 4-member council; S = Supreme Court at Calcutta; C = Court of Directors to report to British Government.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly recalls the four pillars of the 1773 Act.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Remember that Warren Hastings had NO veto power under the 1773 Act. He only had a casting vote when there was a tie. Veto power came much later through the Amendment Act of 1786.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that the Regulating Act 1773 gave the Governor-General veto power over his council. This is FALSE. Warren Hastings was often outvoted 3:1 by his council members (Philip Francis, Clavering, Monson) and possessed only a casting vote.

Examiner Trap: Candidates often confuse the Supreme Court established by the 1773 Act with the Federal Court (1935) or Supreme Court of India (1950). The 1773 Supreme Court was solely for Calcutta and British subjects/designated territories in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

Mains Value Addition: Use keywords like 'Parliamentary oversight', 'transition from merchant to sovereign', 'centralizing impulse', and 'institutional friction' to critically evaluate the evolution of Indian constitutional framework in GS Paper-2.

keyTakeaways: The Regulating Act 1773 was the first statutory acknowledgment of British parliamentary control over Indian affairs and the EIC.
It established structural centralization by elevating the Governor of Bengal to Governor-General and subordinating Bombay and Madras.
Inherent flaws like council deadlocks and jurisdictional clashes with the Supreme Court paved the way for the Act of Settlement 1781 and Pitt's India Act 1784.
